Hands Free Hectare

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
..........farming using only robots and autonomous vehicles to do the work.

Unique Selling Point:
This is cutting edge technology in agrculture.

Summary:
Researchers in the United Kingdom have successfully grown the world's first crop of barley using nothing but robot tractors and drones. The project's aim was to have no operators in the driving seats of the machines or have any agronomists set foot into the 1-hectare paddock.

Further information:
esearchers in the United Kingdom have successfully grown the world's first crop of barley using nothing but robot tractors and drones.

The project's aim was to have no operators in the driving seats of the machines or have any agronomists set foot into the 1-hectare paddock.

Researcher Martin Abell said there was a lot of farming already automated, such as GPS steering, but it was rare to grow an entire crop without anyone stepping into the paddock.

Hence the name of the project — Hands Free Hectare.

Mr Abell said the crop was seeded, sprayed, monitored and harvested autonomously, and it is something farmers could be doing soon.

"We have been able to show the public that this is something that isn't too far ahead in the future, and it could be happening now," he said.

"It has also allowed us to raise the perception of agriculture to the public, so they see it as a forward-thinking industry and something that might attract new people to the industry."


Drone technology automates processes
Researchers used drone technology to automate small agricultural machines, such as tractors and chaser bins.

They also used drones to monitor and bring samples for agronomists to check.

"They were essentially our eyes, so we would assess the field using a multi-spectral camera and get imagery from the field showing us where it was strongest and weakest," Mr Abell said.

"We would then send a little ground rover that would collect samples for us that we could conduct agronomy on.

"And this meant we aren't walking out and on the crop as much, therefore protecting the crop a bit more."

A man wearing earmuffs sitting in a control room looking a computer monitors, with windows and a paddock in the background.
Researcher Martin Abell checks the data from the Hands Free Hectare paddock. (Supplied: Hands Free Hectare)
To get the tractors to work for seeding and harvest, the researchers used an autopilot from a drone, which Mr Abell said was unconventional for research.

"We only had a year to do this project so we had to pick something that didn't require much development," he said.

"It also brought its problems, because the navigation algorithms within a drone are vastly different from those conventionally used for the auto steers on tractors to drive in straight lines.

"So we had to adapt that system to work like an auto steer system and achieve those straight lines that farmers are familiar with."

More testing needed to scale up
After a year of growing, monitoring and harvesting the crop of barley, the researchers were able to show the future of farming could be completely automated.

But there is still plenty of work and testing to be done on a larger scale.

Mr Abell said they were able to prove it could be feasible because part of the project was to do it on a small budget.

"It was roughly $350,000 we had and that was also to hire three people's time, as well as all the equipment we had to buy.

"I am sure if we can make it happen on that budget they can do it commercially with something that is user-friendly for farmers."

Two harvesters in a crop of barley.
The barley crop was harvested completely hands-free. (Supplied: Hands Free Hectare)
Mr Abell said the barley that was grown in the Hands Free Hectare would be put to good use.

"We are currently getting our barley malted to produce a hands-free beer and it is in the process at the moment," he said.

"So hopefully in a couple of months we will have a hands-free beer, which will be nice finish to the project, to celebrate drinking some of that."

----------------------------------

The ground-breaking Hands Free Hectare (HFHa), run by Harper Adams University and Precision Decisions, which aimed to be the first in the world to plant, tend and harvest a crop with only autonomous vehicles and drones, has come to an end after a successful harvest.
The Iseki tractor which was used earlier in the project for the spraying, drilling and rolling, was smaller and lighter than most tractors used nowadays. The team’s mentality that smaller is better was carried through to harvest which was completed with a combine harvester designed to harvest trial plots. The team believe that the use of smaller agricultural machines could improve soil and plant health.
Jonathan Gill, researcher at Harper Adams University, said: “There’s been a focus in recent years on making farming more precise, but the larger machines that we’re using are not compatible with this method of working. They’re also so heavy that their damaging farmers’ soils.
“If combines in the future were similar to the size of the combine we used in this project, which was a little Sampo combine with a header unit of only two meters, it would allow more precise yield maps to be created. They would also be much lighter machines.
“The weather can be an issue when farming, and provide only small windows for work to be completed; we’ve experienced it ourselves with this project. Just like anywhere in the UK, we’ve had to adjust our spraying times and harvest times due to the rain. This is part of the reason machines have been getting so much bigger over the years; we need to be able to complete work quickly. We believe the best solution is that in the future, farmers will manage fleets of smaller, autonomous vehicles. These will be able to go out and work in the fields, allowing the farmer to use their time more effectively and economically instead of having to drive up and down the fields.
“But it’s going to take new talent entering the industry to develop the technology. We hope that this project has helped to inspire some people and shown them the range of interesting and innovative jobs that are available now in agriculture.”
Martin Abell, mechatronics researcher for the industry lead, Precision Decisions, said: “This project aimed to prove that there’s no technological reason why a field can’t be farmed without humans working the land directly now and we’ve done that. We set-out to identify the opportunities for farming and to prove that it’s possible to autonomously farm the land, and that’s been the great success of the project.
“We achieved this on an impressively low budget compared to other projects looking at creating autonomous farming vehicles. The whole project cost less than £200k, funded by Precision Decisions and Innovate UK. We used machinery that was readily available for farmers to buy; open source technology; and an autopilot from a drone for the navigation system.”
Jonathan added: “Despite our combine being 25 years old, it performed absolutely wonderfully.
“It’s phenomenal to know that I was part of this world-first project. To know that we’ve actually done it and you can now look out at the field and see it’s all gone. We grew it, nursed it and now we’ve harvested it, completely autonomously. What an achievement.”
“It feels amazing to have finished,” said Martin. “We’ve worked all year for this. At some points it didn’t feel like it was ever going to happen, but we’ve done it.
“Our major challenge leading up to harvest was getting the combine ready. We spent a lot of time practising; getting our headland turns right and on the day they appeared to be perfect, which was amazing to see.
“The combine drove a lot better than the tractor. We made a bit of a breakthrough with that. Unfortunately, we didn’t have the time to make the same adaptions to our tractor, so even though we’d practised a rolling team, as a precaution during the actual trial, we didn't allow the tractor to get too close to the combine to avoid any accidents.
“Throughout the year we’ve been predicting a yield of 5 tonnes. Looking in the trailer, it looks like we’re not quite there. Our agronomist predicted 4.5 tonnes and it looks like he’s on the money.”
The team now plan to make a Hands Free Hectare beer with the spring barley that has been harvested. They also hope to bring the project back by repeating the experiment, but with a winter crop.
Anyone who is interested in the project and wants to help keep it alive for 2018, please get in contact with the Hands Free Hectare team.

Press Release:


Driven by the need to improve harvests and farm more precisely and efficiently, British scientists are the first to test if in this modern age, hands-free farming is actually possible. Carte Blanche reports from the United Kingdom where an entire crop has been produced without any human intervention in the field and with robots and autonomous vehicles doing all the work.

Script:


V/O:
What you are seeing here is the future of agriculture. Over the last year something incredible has taken place on this hectare of farmland – a world first that could fundamentally change farming as we know it. This piece of land in Shropshire, England is known as the Hands Free Hectare.
Kit Franklin
The Hands Free hectare is the world’s first crop that was grown from establishment through to harvest with no human intervention in the field – autonomous machines doing all of the work.
V/O:
Kit Franklin in the driving force behind this remarkable project. He is a researcher at Harper Adams University where the piece of land known the Hands Free Hectare is located.
LINK:
It is really something to stand here and look at this crop of winter wheat and to realise that it has been planted and is now thriving and yet, it has been untouched by human hands.
V/O:
And this is no exaggeration. For the last 16 months this piece of land has been worked entirely by autonomous machines, robots and drones. Even the harvesting was done autonomously. It all started a little more than a year ago when Franklin’s long-standing interest in the use of robotics in agriculture got the better of him.
Kit:
There has been loads of conversations around agri-robotics for the last 15 years or so, a lot of them highlighting the potential benefit, so if you did not have to have someone driving the machine, the machine could be smaller, smarter, more precise, do less damage to the soils, but the conversation got a bit stagnated and I was really passionate to move that conversation forward.
V/O:
To make this a reality, Franklin approached Clive Blacker, a leading expert in farm automation with the idea of growing a crop completely without human intervention.
Clive:
The concept of robotics is something that is really exciting. We have been involved with automation and auto steers for some time and I firmly believe that robots will have some role to play in the future of agriculture. And just more precise application opportunities that they will present us, will mean that farmers will grow crops far more ethically, sustainably and with significantly higher yields.
V/O:
Blacker jumped at the opportunity to be part of the Hands Free Hectare. The University supported the idea, but still, it was quite a challenge.
Clive:
The project we got was only a 12 month project. Bear in mind, everything we achieved with the Hands Free hectare, we did it from scratch. We had nothing before the project started and we had a year to try and complete this.
V/O:
However, what convinced them that it was possible, was the availability of a range of technologies that they could appropriate and adapt for their project. For example, GPS technology makes it possible to pinpoint locations and plan routes, drone technology allows for the remote steering of all kinds of vehicles, a new generation of sensors, lasers and infra-red cameras makes it possible to gather data with enormous precision, and remotely. All of this made what they had in mind, feasible.
Kit:
Fifteen years ago it would have cost you hundreds of thousands to get anywhere near a system that would have done this and a huge team of researchers. Now this technology is accessible. We are a team of three to four people and we can essentially get on the internet and get the technology we need really quickly. So there was a massive interest and also technology coinciding to make what we have done here.
V/O:
Their big challenge was to adapt the available technology to their specific agricultural needs. In the process they sourced useful items from far and wide.
Clive:
Anything you can imagine and what we could get our hands on, and it was extremely varied. When I tell you what we used, you won’t believe how we used imagination and invention to deliver some of the technologies that we needed. So, we made a really bold statement when we started the project and that was that nobody was going to set foot inside that field when we grew that crop. And that meant that we had to do everything remotely. So, the agronomy was done remotely, the understanding of the health of the plants, collecting plant samples, understanding whether it was ready for harvest. So, we used a whole fleet of different machines.
V/O:
This is a small rover developed from a toy to test their remote steering system and to make sure they can control their larger vehicles. This bigger rover started life as an electric wheel chair. They removed the chair and fitted the base with controls, sensors and cameras so that they could send back close-up images of the status of the crop. It even has a scoop to collect soil and pant samples. The tractor they used was automated by using drone technology.
V/O:
We took a completely standard tractor that is operated by a driver. So, it has hand and feet controls, there are levers that lift the linkage up and down on the back which lifts the implements up and down. There is a foot pedal which essentially drives the tractor forwards or backwards, depending on how much us moved. What we did was basically change all those, adapt all those movements with linear actuators, electrical linear actuators that essentially move the levers and they are in turn controlled by this drone technology, this brain from a drone which actually in itself was derived from a mobile phone. So, a mobile phone was taken, developed into a drone. We have taken the drone and developed it into an autonomous tractor. So, we have taken drone technology, we have taken reliable agricultural technology and we brought them together in a way that no one else had thought of doing.
LINK:
The entire automated process is controlled and monitored from this mobile structure which is right next to the Hands Free Hectare. The team refers to it as” Mission Control”
V/O:
The team even had use for a poop scoop.
Clive:
We even used a quadcopter and we were using that with technology such as really basic poop scoop that you would use for picking up after your dog to go in and grab samples of crops heads that we could then pull off and bring back to our mission control centre to we could check the moisture of the crop and suitability for harvest.
V/O:
Their systems were not perfect, and the tractor and harvester did not always run in straight lines. It was learning through trial and error, but in the end, they were able to harvest the barley crop successfully in September last year. The average UK yield is 5 tons per hectare and they managed 4.5 tons, which is great for an experimental farm, run on a shoestring budget.
Kit:
We have been the world’s first to do what we have done in terms of grow a crop through a whole cycle from planting through to harvest and that is world leading. If our technology is world leading? Maybe not. There are other people who have more smart systems but they are still in demonstration phases and they haven’t gotten them into the field. So, we have pushed that conversation by getting actually into the field and actually doing some farming.
V/O:
The project was initially scheduled for only one year, but the amazing success has ensured that the project is continuing.
LINK:
Last year this field was planted with spring barley and in this second season of the Hands Free Hectare winter wheat is being grown here.
V/O:
And Blacker says technology is constantly being developed that would make autonomous farming more precise and viable in future.
Clive:
Stuff that you would never have imagined was possible and achievable is being developed. From sensors that will be able to pick out disease pixels on a leaf to speciate the types of disease. We’ve got sensors that are capable of sniffing the disease out of the air before it actually gets to the plant.
V/O:
All of this makes the ultimate aim of the teams much more feasible in the very near future.
Kit:
The plan is bigger and better things. We want to do a hands-free farm which will be multiple fields, multiple crops, all managed from an office. Remote agronomy, so field sensors and machines that essentially drive themselves from the yard out to the field to do the job and return.
V/O:
When we visited the Hands-Free Hectare, there was an event focused on the project. They also unveiled a special drink created from the first Hands Free barley crop that celebrates the dawn of an entirely new kind of farming.

Kit: There has been loads of conversations around agri-robotics for the last 15 years or so, a lot of them highlighting the potential benefit, so if you did not have to have someone driving the machine, the machine could be smaller, smarter, more precise, do less damage to the soils, but the conversation got a bit stagnated and I was really passionate to move that conversation forward. V/O: To make this a reality, Franklin approached Clive Blacker, a leading expert in farm automation with the idea of growing a crop completely without human intervention. Clive: The concept of robotics is something that is really exciting. We have been involved with automation and auto steers for some time and I firmly believe that robots will have some role to play in the future of agriculture. And just more precise application opportunities that they will present us, will mean that farmers will grow crops far more ethically, sustainably and with significantly higher yields. V/O: Blacker jumped at the opportunity to be part of the Hands Free Hectare. The University supported the idea, but still, it was quite a challenge. Clive: The project we got was only a 12 month project. Bear in mind, everything we achieved with the Hands Free hectare, we did it from scratch. We had nothing before the project started and we had a year to try and complete this. V/O: However, what convinced them that it was possible, was the availability of a range of technologies that they could appropriate and adapt for their project. For example, GPS technology makes it possible to pinpoint locations and plan routes, drone technology allows for the remote steering of all kinds of vehicles, a new generation of sensors, lasers and infra-red cameras makes it possible to gather data with enormous precision, and remotely. All of this made what they had in mind, feasible. Kit: Fifteen years ago it would have cost you hundreds of thousands to get anywhere near a system that would have done this and a huge team of researchers. Now this technology is accessible. We are a team of three to four people and we can essentially get on the internet and get the technology we need really quickly. So there was a massive interest and also technology coinciding to make what we have done here. V/O: Their big challenge was to adapt the available technology to their specific agricultural needs. In the process they sourced useful items from far and wide. Clive: Anything you can imagine and what we could get our hands on, and it was extremely varied. When I tell you what we used, you won’t believe how we used imagination and invention to deliver some of the technologies that we needed. So, we made a really bold statement when we started the project and that was that nobody was going to set foot inside that field when we grew that crop. And that meant that we had to do everything remotely. So, the agronomy was done remotely, the understanding of the health of the plants, collecting plant samples, understanding whether it was ready for harvest. So, we used a whole fleet of different machines. V/O: This is a small rover developed from a toy to test their remote steering system and to make sure they can control their larger vehicles. This bigger rover started life as an electric wheel chair. They removed the chair and fitted the base with controls, sensors and cameras so that they could send back close-up images of the status of the crop. It even has a scoop to collect soil and pant samples. The tractor they used was automated by using drone technology. V/O: We took a completely standard tractor that is operated by a driver. So, it has hand and feet controls, there are levers that lift the linkage up and down on the back which lifts the implements up and down. There is a foot pedal which essentially drives the tractor forwards or backwards, depending on how much us moved. What we did was basically change all those, adapt all those movements with linear actuators, electrical linear actuators that essentially move the levers and they are in turn controlled by this drone technology, this brain from a drone which actually in itself was derived from a mobile phone. So, a mobile phone was taken, developed into a drone. We have taken the drone and developed it into an autonomous tractor. So, we have taken drone technology, we have taken reliable agricultural technology and we brought them together in a way that no one else had thought of doing. LINK: The entire automated process is controlled and monitored from this mobile structure which is right next to the Hands Free Hectare. The team refers to it as” Mission Control” V/O: The team even had use for a poop scoop. Clive: We even used a quadcopter and we were using that with technology such as really basic poop scoop that you would use for picking up after your dog to go in and grab samples of crops heads that we could then pull off and bring back to our mission control centre to we could check the moisture of the crop and suitability for harvest. V/O: Their systems were not perfect, and the tractor and harvester did not always run in straight lines. It was learning through trial and error, but in the end, they were able to harvest the barley crop successfully in September last year. The average UK yield is 5 tons per hectare and they managed 4.5 tons, which is great for an experimental farm, run on a shoestring budget. Kit: We have been the world’s first to do what we have done in terms of grow a crop through a whole cycle from planting through to harvest and that is world leading. If our technology is world leading? Maybe not. There are other people who have more smart systems but they are still in demonstration phases and they haven’t gotten them into the field. So, we have pushed that conversation by getting actually into the field and actually doing some farming. V/O: The project was initially scheduled for only one year, but the amazing success has ensured that the project is continuing. LINK: Last year this field was planted with spring barley and in this second season of the Hands Free Hectare winter wheat is being grown here. V/O: And Blacker says technology is constantly being developed that would make autonomous farming more precise and viable in future. Clive: Stuff that you would never have imagined was possible and achievable is being developed. From sensors that will be able to pick out disease pixels on a leaf to speciate the types of disease. We’ve got sensors that are capable of sniffing the disease out of the air before it actually gets to the plant. V/O: All of this makes the ultimate aim of the teams much more feasible in the very near future. Kit: The plan is bigger and better things. We want to do a hands-free farm which will be multiple fields, multiple crops, all managed from an office. Remote agronomy, so field sensors and machines that essentially drive themselves from the yard out to the field to do the job and return. V/O: When we visited the Hands-Free Hectare, there was an event focused on the project. They also unveiled a special drink created from the first Hands Free barley crop that celebrates the dawn of an entirely new kind of farming.

metadata.Summary: Researchers in the United Kingdom have successfully grown the world's first crop of barley using nothing but robot tractors and drones. The project's aim was to have no operators in the driving seats of the machines or have any agronomists set foot into the 1-hectare paddock.
metadata.Further information: esearchers in the United Kingdom have successfully grown the world's first crop of barley using nothing but robot tractors and drones. The project's aim was to have no operators in the driving seats of the machines or have any agronomists set foot into the 1-hectare paddock. Researcher Martin Abell said there was a lot of farming already automated, such as GPS steering, but it was rare to grow an entire crop without anyone stepping into the paddock. Hence the name of the project — Hands Free Hectare. Mr Abell said the crop was seeded, sprayed, monitored and harvested autonomously, and it is something farmers could be doing soon. "We have been able to show the public that this is something that isn't too far ahead in the future, and it could be happening now," he said. "It has also allowed us to raise the perception of agriculture to the public, so they see it as a forward-thinking industry and something that might attract new people to the industry." Drone technology automates processes Researchers used drone technology to automate small agricultural machines, such as tractors and chaser bins. They also used drones to monitor and bring samples for agronomists to check. "They were essentially our eyes, so we would assess the field using a multi-spectral camera and get imagery from the field showing us where it was strongest and weakest," Mr Abell said. "We would then send a little ground rover that would collect samples for us that we could conduct agronomy on. "And this meant we aren't walking out and on the crop as much, therefore protecting the crop a bit more." A man wearing earmuffs sitting in a control room looking a computer monitors, with windows and a paddock in the background. Researcher Martin Abell checks the data from the Hands Free Hectare paddock. (Supplied: Hands Free Hectare) To get the tractors to work for seeding and harvest, the researchers used an autopilot from a drone, which Mr Abell said was unconventional for research. "We only had a year to do this project so we had to pick something that didn't require much development," he said. "It also brought its problems, because the navigation algorithms within a drone are vastly different from those conventionally used for the auto steers on tractors to drive in straight lines. "So we had to adapt that system to work like an auto steer system and achieve those straight lines that farmers are familiar with." More testing needed to scale up After a year of growing, monitoring and harvesting the crop of barley, the researchers were able to show the future of farming could be completely automated. But there is still plenty of work and testing to be done on a larger scale. Mr Abell said they were able to prove it could be feasible because part of the project was to do it on a small budget. "It was roughly $350,000 we had and that was also to hire three people's time, as well as all the equipment we had to buy. "I am sure if we can make it happen on that budget they can do it commercially with something that is user-friendly for farmers." Two harvesters in a crop of barley. The barley crop was harvested completely hands-free. (Supplied: Hands Free Hectare) Mr Abell said the barley that was grown in the Hands Free Hectare would be put to good use. "We are currently getting our barley malted to produce a hands-free beer and it is in the process at the moment," he said. "So hopefully in a couple of months we will have a hands-free beer, which will be nice finish to the project, to celebrate drinking some of that." ---------------------------------- The ground-breaking Hands Free Hectare (HFHa), run by Harper Adams University and Precision Decisions, which aimed to be the first in the world to plant, tend and harvest a crop with only autonomous vehicles and drones, has come to an end after a successful harvest. The Iseki tractor which was used earlier in the project for the spraying, drilling and rolling, was smaller and lighter than most tractors used nowadays. The team’s mentality that smaller is better was carried through to harvest which was completed with a combine harvester designed to harvest trial plots. The team believe that the use of smaller agricultural machines could improve soil and plant health. Jonathan Gill, researcher at Harper Adams University, said: “There’s been a focus in recent years on making farming more precise, but the larger machines that we’re using are not compatible with this method of working. They’re also so heavy that their damaging farmers’ soils. “If combines in the future were similar to the size of the combine we used in this project, which was a little Sampo combine with a header unit of only two meters, it would allow more precise yield maps to be created. They would also be much lighter machines. “The weather can be an issue when farming, and provide only small windows for work to be completed; we’ve experienced it ourselves with this project. Just like anywhere in the UK, we’ve had to adjust our spraying times and harvest times due to the rain. This is part of the reason machines have been getting so much bigger over the years; we need to be able to complete work quickly. We believe the best solution is that in the future, farmers will manage fleets of smaller, autonomous vehicles. These will be able to go out and work in the fields, allowing the farmer to use their time more effectively and economically instead of having to drive up and down the fields. “But it’s going to take new talent entering the industry to develop the technology. We hope that this project has helped to inspire some people and shown them the range of interesting and innovative jobs that are available now in agriculture.” Martin Abell, mechatronics researcher for the industry lead, Precision Decisions, said: “This project aimed to prove that there’s no technological reason why a field can’t be farmed without humans working the land directly now and we’ve done that. We set-out to identify the opportunities for farming and to prove that it’s possible to autonomously farm the land, and that’s been the great success of the project. “We achieved this on an impressively low budget compared to other projects looking at creating autonomous farming vehicles. The whole project cost less than £200k, funded by Precision Decisions and Innovate UK. We used machinery that was readily available for farmers to buy; open source technology; and an autopilot from a drone for the navigation system.” Jonathan added: “Despite our combine being 25 years old, it performed absolutely wonderfully. “It’s phenomenal to know that I was part of this world-first project. To know that we’ve actually done it and you can now look out at the field and see it’s all gone. We grew it, nursed it and now we’ve harvested it, completely autonomously. What an achievement.” “It feels amazing to have finished,” said Martin. “We’ve worked all year for this. At some points it didn’t feel like it was ever going to happen, but we’ve done it. “Our major challenge leading up to harvest was getting the combine ready. We spent a lot of time practising; getting our headland turns right and on the day they appeared to be perfect, which was amazing to see. “The combine drove a lot better than the tractor. We made a bit of a breakthrough with that. Unfortunately, we didn’t have the time to make the same adaptions to our tractor, so even though we’d practised a rolling team, as a precaution during the actual trial, we didn't allow the tractor to get too close to the combine to avoid any accidents. “Throughout the year we’ve been predicting a yield of 5 tonnes. Looking in the trailer, it looks like we’re not quite there. Our agronomist predicted 4.5 tonnes and it looks like he’s on the money.” The team now plan to make a Hands Free Hectare beer with the spring barley that has been harvested. They also hope to bring the project back by repeating the experiment, but with a winter crop. Anyone who is interested in the project and wants to help keep it alive for 2018, please get in contact with the Hands Free Hectare team.
